about.roleCategory: IT ANALYST · HEADING TOWARD BACKEND, WITH APPLIED AI
bioParagraphs: I am an IT Analyst at Grupo GVS and a Software Engineering undergraduate at Pontifícia Universidade Católica de Minas Gerais (PUC Minas). I build applications that solve real problems, with AI as support, and I also handle their backend: that is where I want to take my career, as a backend developer.

I believe building good software goes beyond writing functional code: it is about delivering pleasant, intuitive, and purpose-driven products. I cultivate a disciplined routine of continuous learning, diving deep into computer science fundamentals, object-oriented programming with Java, and the modern web ecosystem with JavaScript and React.

I operate natively with Artificial Intelligence, leveraging cutting-edge AI models and developer agents to explore novel ideas, rapidly prototype solutions, debug complex architectures, and sustain a productive engineering workflow, always applying critical judgment over code elegance and maintainability.

degraueduca.title: Degrau Educa
degraueduca.tagline: Climb each step of your career with purpose.
degraueduca.intro: A web platform that gathers free vocational courses from recognized institutions and organizes them into paths: courses in order, from the first one to a first job, with each student's progress saved.

meta.value: Design Thinking and UX, the admin panel with 4 CRUDs and part of sign-up and login

problem.title: Free courses are everywhere. Knowing which ones are worth it, and in what order, is not.
problem.body: Getting into the job market today takes more than a high school diploma. Platforms offer countless courses, and picking one, or planning a sequence of studies, becomes hard. With free courses it is worse: there is no way to tell which ones are good and recognized by employers.

quotes.label: What surprised us most
quotes.text: The rise in employability and average salary of people who take vocational courses, and the lack of tools that help place those courses on a résumé.

quotes.label: What mattered most
quotes.text: Studying online is widely accepted, and similar solutions exist that can serve as references.

quotes.label: Left to investigate
quotes.text: Which learning platforms and associations employers value most when choosing a candidate.

problem.note: Summary of the team's research highlights board.
problem.goal: Bring free courses from recognized platforms into one place, classify them by area of interest and chain them into paths with a logical, progressive sequence.

research.title: Before code, separate what we know from what we assume.
research.body: The process followed Design Thinking on Miro, from a template provided by the professors: a CSD Matrix to align certainties, assumptions and doubts, a stakeholder map, research, and personas with empathy maps and value propositions.

csd.label: Certainties
items: Institutions like SENAC, SESC, Udemy, Fundação Bradesco, USP and FGV offer free courses
These courses are not promoted in one central place

csd.label: Assumptions
items: Courses help people get into the job market
Tracking progress during a course makes a difference

csd.label: Doubts
items: How many students does the market actually hire?
What makes a student give up?
What age group looks for these courses?

research.csdAlt: CSD Alignment Matrix with the columns Doubts, Certainties and Assumptions
research.csdCaption: CSD Matrix: the doubts became research questions.
research.stakeholdersAlt: Stakeholder map in three circles: fundamental, important and influencers
research.stakeholdersCaption: Stakeholder map: students and learning platforms at the center; employers and the Ministry of Education at the edge.

personas.name: Lucas, 19
personas.role: Student looking for a first job
personas.want: Find free courses, improve his résumé and land a first job.
personas.pain: Too many options, no direction and low motivation: starts courses and drops them.
personas.design: Ready-made paths, plain language and encouragement along the way.

personas.name: Juliana, 32
personas.want: A promotion and new skills without leaving her job.
personas.pain: Lack of time, fatigue and trouble staying consistent.
personas.design: Focused courses, workload in plain sight and progress that picks up where she left off.

personas.name: Carlos, 28
personas.want: A job and practical skills to improve his life.
personas.pain: Phone-only access, limited internet and little familiarity with technology.
personas.design: A light, responsive, inclusive interface without jargon.

design.title: User stories, wireframes and a prototype before coding.
design.body: The personas became user stories in the "As a… I need… so that…" format and one value proposition each. From them came wireframes for five screens (home, login, profile, course and path), the user flow and a clickable prototype, used to validate navigation before writing code.

admin.title: A panel to grow the catalog without touching code.
admin.body: Admins use the same login and land on a panel with four modules in the side menu. Each one is a CRUD over a JSON Server collection, using fetch with GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE, and an on-screen notice after every operation.

modules.title: Partners
modules.text: List, Create, Edit and Delete tabs. The list filters the table as you type; Edit suggests partners by name and fills the form; Delete removes several at once, with "select all".

modules.alt: Edit form for the Algorithms and Programming Logic course with every field filled in

modules.title: Paths

modules.alt: Editing the Python path: checked courses and the Order of selected courses list with up and down arrows

modules.title: Motivational messages
modules.text: Encouraging messages fired by triggers: consecutive login days, total logins, finishing a course or a path, clicks and progress percentage.
modules.alt: Motivational Messages module with the event type and quantity form and the table of saved messages

code.title: Reordering a course in a path
code.text: Swaps the course with its neighbor and redraws the list; the arrows at the ends stay disabled.

code.title: Slug from the title
code.text: Strips accents and symbols to build the course address: "Lógica de Programação" becomes "logica-de-programacao".

code.title: Login that counts consecutive days
code.text: Every login adds to the total, but the streak only grows when the last visit was on another day. It feeds the dashboard and the messages.

admin.loginNote: In sign-up and login, I also worked on account creation (with password confirmation and a sequential id), the login that updates total visits and the day streak, and the redirect by profile: students to the dashboard, admins to the panel.

data.title: Seven collections and a mocked REST API.
data.body: No custom backend: JSON Server turns a JSON file into a REST API and serves the site's files. Collections link by id, and the logged-in user lives in localStorage.

stack.title: Plain web, from prototype to hosting.
stack.process: Planning was done together, with Scrum and Design Thinking. During development, each member took specific screens and CRUDs; merging the modules was done as a group again.

next.title: What I would do differently today.

items.title: Server-side authentication
items.text: Passwords are stored in plain text in the JSON file and login is checked in the browser. In a product, that moves to the server, with password hashing and sessions.

items.title: Feedback on the page
items.text: Replace alert() with messages next to the field that failed and ask for confirmation before deleting several records at once.

items.title: Tests for the CRUDs
items.text: Automated tests for the panel's operations, so merging the modules would not depend on checking everything by hand.

closing.title: Organizing the path is teaching too.
closing.text: Degrau Educa does not create courses: it picks the good ones and says in which order to take them. It was my first complete web project as part of a team, from personas to the panel that keeps it all running.

sentinelagvs.docTitle: Sentinela GVS, case study | Victor Cândido Leite
sentinelagvs.title: Sentinela GVS
sentinelagvs.tagline: AI that watches the plants around the clock and alerts the team within 2 seconds.
sentinelagvs.intro: An in-house system, requested by the Operations & Maintenance (O&M) team of Grupo GVS's solar plants, that watches every camera at once and only calls the team when a person is where they shouldn't be, with photo and video on their phones within seconds.
sentinelagvs.status: In production at Grupo GVS · since October 2026

meta.label: Company
meta.value: Grupo GVS · solar power generation · requested by Operations & Maintenance (O&M) · October 2026, ongoing

meta.label: My role
meta.value: Lead developer: most features and non-functional requirements (performance, availability, security and privacy)

sentinelagvs.coverAlt: Sentinela GVS panel with the list of plants and cameras and a live camera marking "person 89%" inside the watched zone
sentinelagvs.demoNote: Every screen and the video come from an isolated demo instance: plants, cameras, user and incidents are fictional, and the people come from free-license Pexels videos. No real footage of the plants appears here.

problem.title: A recording camera is not security if nobody is watching.
problem.body: The need came from the Operations & Maintenance (O&M) team. Solar plants sit on large rural sites far from any staff, and cable and equipment theft is a real risk: it interrupts generation, adds replacement costs and hits revenue. Cameras were already recording, but nobody can watch dozens of feeds all night; in practice, footage only helped find out what had happened after the loss.
constraints: Know as it happens, not the next day.
Using the limited internet the plants already have.

solution.title: Watch every camera and only call when it matters.
solution.body: A person-detection AI runs locally on the video from every camera. Each incident becomes a record with photo and video that reaches the team's phones and enters a response panel.

features.title: Business-rule zones
features.text: Each camera has the area that matters (fence, gate, inverters) and the hours when the alarm is armed. Outside that, it bothers no one.

features.title: Phone alert in seconds
features.text: Photo and video of the incident reach the team on Telegram, starting 5 seconds before the person entered.

features.title: Organized response
features.text: The operator classifies each incident (authorized person, false alarm or real intrusion) and follows a real intrusion until it is solved.

features.title: Evidence ready for the police
features.text: The original HD video is pulled from the recorder in one click, for the police report.

features.title: Data for management
features.text: Automatic weekly and monthly PDF reports, a KPI dashboard and a view for the control-room TVs.

features.title: Privacy by design (LGPD)
features.text: False-alarm media is deleted within 24 hours; access only from the internal network, with role-based login.

flow.ai: AI detects a person in the armed zone and schedule
flow.recorderNote: original video for the police report
flow.omNote: needs and alarm rules for the panel

role.title: Operations define the needs; I build.
role.body: The project started as an O&M request, and O&M defines what operations need. My lead works with me to keep those needs up to date as operations evolve. I build most of the features and most of the non-functional requirements.
items: Features: detection, per-camera alarm rules, incidents and triage, alerts, reports and the UI.
Performance to fit many cameras on one machine, with the same GPU.
Access security and data privacy, from day one.
Taking part in designing the expansion that moves processing to each plant.

challenge.title: Many cameras, a weak link and a single computer.
challenge.body: Plant internet links only supported detection on 4 or 5 cameras at a time; the rest were blind. The way video travels was reorganized: each plant got a bandwidth budget, and high-quality recording stays on the local recorder. That brought every camera online. Then the AI was optimized so the same computer could handle much more.
challenge.tableTitle: AI optimization on the same computer
rows: Estimated capacity on the same computer
challenge.dogs: Dogs were being mistaken for people. The operation's own false alarms were used to test AI models and pick the best one: dogs mistaken for people dropped from 8 to 2 out of 17 cases, and real-person detection improved.

results.title: One month of operation, across three plants.
results.body: From Oct 5 to Nov 6, 2026, with all 54 cameras at the three plants.
rows: Incidents logged and delivered to the team
Classified incidents confirmed as real people
Time from detection to phone alert
Video the team needs to review
274 h of incidents, instead of a month of continuous recording from every camera

roadmap.title: One computer per plant and a central hub.
roadmap.body: The system is moving to one computer per plant plus a central hub: each plant analyzes its own cameras and sends only incidents, which takes the load off the network and allows growth to new plants without replacing the hub. Updates are published centrally and roll back automatically if something goes wrong. A pilot at one plant runs in parallel with current operations.
roadmap.pilot: From the pilot: without a dedicated GPU, the plant caught only 65% of person incidents. So every new plant gets one.

items.title: Keep the business close
items.text: Alarm rules, triage and reports came from O&M's daily routine, not from assumptions.

items.title: Measure before changing
items.text: The biggest gain did not come from swapping the AI: the network and video decoding weighed more than the artificial intelligence.

items.title: Real data and privacy from the start
items.text: The operation's own false alarms became the test for choosing the model, and treating LGPD as a requirement from day one helped the system get adopted.

stack.title: Local AI, no cloud.
stack.process: Everything runs on a company computer with an NVIDIA GPU: detection, the web panel on the internal network, alerts and reports.

closing.title: From an operations request to a production system.
closing.text: O&M brought the need; I built most of the system: the AI, the rules, the screens, the alerts, the reports and what keeps it all running 24/7. It is the project where technology most clearly turned into business results.

wisptv.docTitle: WISP TV, case study | Victor Cândido Leite
wisptv.title: WISP TV
wisptv.tagline: The operations systems straight on the TVs, with no computer in between.
wisptv.intro: An app installed on each TV at Grupo GVS's Operations Center that turns it into a terminal for the plant dashboards: it opens by itself on power-up, keeps each TV on its screen, recovers from network drops and follows commands from the operators.
wisptv.status: In production at Grupo GVS · since October 2026

meta.label: Company
meta.value: Grupo GVS · solar plant Operations Center · October 2026

meta.label: Scale
meta.value: 8 TVs in the office, 5 running the app; 7 screens by remote

meta.label: My role
meta.value: Developer and technical owner: requirements, AI-assisted development, acceptance testing and rollout

wisptv.coverAlt: WISP TV menu with the Operations Center logo and seven screen cards, SCREEN 1 marked as pinned and SCREEN 4 in focus
wisptv.demoNote: Every screen and the video come from the app itself (v1.8) running on the official Android TV emulator, pointed at a demo server: plants, TVs and alerts are fictional. The command page is a mock-up with the same API contract; nothing was captured from production.

problem.title: The operations TVs lost their source.
problem.body: The Operations Center monitors the plants through web systems: generation, alert and monitoring dashboards. So the team could see everything at a glance, those screens reached the office TVs through two computers wired to them. When those computers were needed for daily work, the TVs went blank. The dashboards had to go straight to the TV.

options.title: Casting (Chromecast)
options.text: No remote control support and low-resolution rendering.

options.title: The TV's browser
options.text: Opened the page, but did not come back after a power outage or survive someone pressing the wrong remote.

options.title: Dedicated devices
options.text: Purchase cost plus more equipment on the network to maintain.

solution.title: A TV that behaves like operations equipment.
solution.body: A purpose-built app installed on each TV, with no third-party libraries so the in-house team can maintain it.

features.title: Menu on the remote
features.text: 7 screens (5 plant dashboards, 1 alerts and 1 generation monitoring), picked with arrows and OK; arrows also cycle between them.

features.title: Opens by itself on power-up
features.text: After standby or a power outage, the TV returns to its screen without anyone touching it.

features.title: Pinned screen per TV
features.text: Each TV has its own screen. If someone moves it away, it returns after 5 idle minutes.

features.title: Operator control
features.text: From a web page, the operator reloads a TV or sends it back to its screen in one click, with no technician.

features.title: Screens that fit the TV
features.text: A dashboard made for desktop monitors is scaled and centred by an injected script, rechecked every 30 seconds.

features.title: Network recovery
features.text: If a page fails to load, the app says so and retries every 30 seconds.

flow.tv: TV + WISP TV app: menu, pinned screen and watchdog
flow.operator: Operator: reload or send back to the pinned screen
flow.poll: The TV asks every ~15 s whether there is a command for it; the server never connects to the TV.

challenge.title: Making a consumer TV behave like operations equipment.
challenge.body: Consumer TVs are built for living rooms: they save power, close "forgotten" apps and obey any remote. In an operations office, all of that gets in the way.

items.title: The TV would not let the app start by itself
items.text: A manufacturer "protector" blocks the boot broadcast (BOOT_COMPLETED) and kills services started at boot. At boot the app now only schedules a system alarm (AlarmManager), which the protector allows; once the screen opens, it starts the watchdog service.

items.title: Stray remotes pulled TVs off their screen
items.text: Android does not let one app see what happens in others. The rule that does not need to: off the pinned screen for 5 idle minutes, the TV goes back. And to avoid opening behind the screensaver, the app wakes the TV first (wake lock).

items.title: Fixing a TV required a technician
items.text: Each TV asks the operations dashboard every ~15 s whether there is a command for it, acknowledges it on the next request and never repeats a command. If the dashboard is down, the TV keeps showing what it shows and retries every 60 s.

items.title: The TV lied about its screen size
items.text: The embedded browser reported 1431×805 while the visible area was 961×541, and one dashboard overflowed. The app corrects those values after load. Same investigation: the TV renders its whole UI at 1280×720 despite a Full HD panel.

challenge.tableTitle: Before and after, measured in acceptance testing
rows: none: the app runs on the TV
stayed off until someone stepped in
open by themselves in ~105 s (only ~6 s is the app)
TV moved away by another remote

results.title: Two weeks, eight releases, five TVs.
results.body: Figures from the acceptance and rollout records, Oct 14–27, 2026.
rows: Computers freed up for daily work
TVs running the app in production
8 in about 2 weeks, each validated on a test TV
4 of 4 interference scenarios, between 5 min 05 s and 5 min 34 s
8 of 8, including server down, expired command and unidentified TV
zero: the TVs were already there

role.title: From operations requirements to the rollout script.
items: Gathered requirements with the operations team: what each TV must show and how the screens are used.
Built the app from scratch with AI assistance: I defined the behaviour, reviewed the code and ran the tests on real TVs. No third-party libraries, so the in-house team can maintain it.
Diagnosed manufacturer and web-page blockers by reading system logs (logcat, dumpsys) and inspecting the WebView live through DevTools.
Wrote and ran acceptance test plans on a test TV before every release, with screenshots and logs.
Defined the command API contract with the operations web dashboard and tested it in staging before production.
Automated rollout with scripts (install, hash-based version check, per-TV configuration) and documented installation and rollback.

roadmap.title: What comes next.
items: Sign the app with the IT department's official key and formalise distribution.
TV-specific versions of the dashboards with larger type (already prototyped: 8 cards per page, rotating).
Evaluate an external device for true Full HD, since the current TVs render their UI at 720p.
TV health indicators (last contact, version) on the command page.

items.title: Measure before optimising
items.text: Finding the 720p render limit saved weeks of pointless tuning in the app.

items.title: Work with the platform
items.text: A system alarm solved what a background service could not.

items.title: Simple rules hold up better
items.text: "5 minutes off the screen, go back" works without seeing what Android hides.

items.title: The TV pulls, the server doesn't push
items.text: Reversing the direction of communication simplified security and made failures harmless.

items.title: AI speeds up, the device decides
items.text: With AI assistance each release took hours, yet three issues only showed up on the real TV.

stack.title: Plain Android, no dependencies.
stack.process: Plain Java on Android TV, with no third-party libraries: a WebView shows the dashboards, a foreground service watches the screen and a system alarm guarantees startup at boot.

closing.title: Equipment that was already there, working on its own.
closing.text: Without buying anything, the office TVs became operations terminals that power on, self-correct and recover on their own, and two computers went back to work.

aluguelcarros.docTitle: Car Rental, case study | Victor Cândido Leite
aluguelcarros.kicker: full stack web system · web development lab · 2026
aluguelcarros.title: Car Rental
aluguelcarros.tagline: From the customer's request to a contract with credit, with every rule enforced by the API.
aluguelcarros.intro: A web system where customers request car rentals and agents, companies and banks, assess those requests financially, execute the contracts and grant credit. A Spring Boot API, a React front end and a Supabase database, from the course assignment to the final verification.

meta.label: Context
meta.value: PUC Minas · Web Application Development and Integration (DIAW) · Lab 02, worth 15 points

meta.label: Scale
meta.value: 3 access roles, 12 screens, 13 tasks, each with an issue and a pull request

meta.label: My role
meta.value: Solo project: UML modeling, API, front end, tests and verification

aluguelcarros.coverAlt: Assessment screen for request 2 from customer Marina Costa: Mercosur plate RTA2F41, request path under review, 13.1% of income committed against the 30% reference, income list and assessment form
aluguelcarros.demoNote: Every screen comes from the system itself running locally, with the development profile's H2 database and the fictitious users created by the initial migration (Marina, João, Locadora Rota Sul and Banco Horizonte, among others). No data is real.

stats.label: API tests, with JUnit 5 and MockMvc
front-end tests, with Vitest and Testing Library
end-to-end flows passing in Chrome and Firefox
screen and width combinations measured, with no failures
color pairs measured, all above minimum contrast

aluguelcarros.statsNote: Measurements from the 2026-11-04 verification, on the production build, at 1440, 900 and 390 px.

problem.title: Request, assess and contract a rental online.
problem.body: The lab asked for a system to place, cancel and modify car rental requests. Customers sign up and send requests; agents, which are companies and banks, assess each request financially and, with a positive assessment, execute the contract. The car is registered as owned by the customer, the company or the bank, depending on the contract, and a bank can attach credit to the rental. The architecture was set too: MVC, with one subsystem for the web pages and another for managing requests and contracts.

actors.title: Customer
actors.text: Registers ID numbers, address, occupation and up to 3 incomes. Creates, views, modifies and cancels their own requests and follows every step.

actors.title: Company
actors.text: An agent that reviews the customer's income, records the assessment, executes the contract and maintains the cars it owns.

actors.title: Bank
actors.text: An agent that also assesses and contracts, and the only one that grants credit: financed amount, monthly interest rate and number of installments.

problem.goal: every rule of the assignment enforced by the API, not just the screen, and every role seeing only what belongs to it.

architecture.title: Model first, then code, and the model revised at the end.
architecture.body: React plays the View and consumes the API as JSON. In Spring Boot, controller is the Controller; service, repository and model form the Model. Packages follow the structure used in the course projects. The diagrams were drawn in PlantUML before the code and revised twice, until version 3 matched the delivered system.
architecture.packagesAlt: Package diagram v3: React web pages subsystem with routes, pages, components, contexts, utils and services, linked by HTTP and JSON to the Spring Boot subsystem with application, config, controller, service, security, exception, repository and model, and to Supabase over JDBC
architecture.packagesCaption: Package diagram (v3): the two MVC subsystems, linked by HTTP and JSON.
architecture.useCasesAlt: Use case diagram v3 with the Customer, Company and Bank actors and the sign-up, requests, assessment, contract, credit and cars use cases
architecture.useCasesCaption: Use cases (v3), the basis for the 13 user stories.
architecture.classesAlt: Class diagram v3: abstract Usuario with Cliente and Agente, Agente specialized into Empresa and Banco, PedidoAluguel with Parecer and Contrato, ContratoCredito, Automovel, Rendimento, Endereco and the Perfil, StatusPedido and TipoContrato enums
architecture.classesCaption: Class diagram (v3): 11 entities and 3 enums, with JOINED inheritance for Usuario. Click to open at full size.
rows: The dto package goes away; application and config come in on the back end
Follow the course projects' structure, with API input and output in model, never exposing the password
Automovel gets valorDiaria and PedidoAluguel gets getValorTotal()
Compute the request's value and the committed income in the assessment
security reads id and role from the JWT itself, without going to repository
The filter authenticates every request without querying the database
Maintenance methods on the entities, such as exigirAlteravel() and associarCredito()
Keep the rules inside the domain instead of spread across services
A utils package on the front end
Gather currency, date and document formatting and each screen's title

lifecycle.title: Six states, and every transition checked.
lifecycle.body: The heart of the system is the request's path. Every state change goes through an entity method that refuses the transition if the request is not in the right state; the API turns that refusal into a clear message on screen.

steps.title: Sent
steps.who: The customer picks the car and the dates

exits.text: Unfavorable assessment: the request leaves the queue, with the justification visible to the customer.
The customer cancels at any time before the contract.

lifecycle.note: Changing the car or the dates of an assessed request warns first, discards the assessment and sends the request back to ENVIADO.
rules: Up to 3 incomes per customer; monthly income is their sum.
Unique login, CPF and RG, with the CPF check digits validated.
The financial profile is shown only to agents, with the committed income and the informative 30% reference.
The car's owner comes from the contract type: the customer, the company that executed it or the bank that financed it.
A company only becomes the owner of a car that is already its own; a bank only becomes the owner by granting credit.
Only the current owner edits or deletes a car, and a car that appears in a request cannot be deleted.
A customer account cannot be deleted with a request in progress or an executed contract.
A customer never sees or changes another customer's request: the API answers as if it did not exist.
lifecycle.codeCycleText: A request only goes under review if it is waiting, and an assessment is only recorded while under review. The final status comes from the assessment itself.
lifecycle.codeContractText: The rule the verification showed was missing: a company could take, through the contract, another company's car. The role test passed; the owner was never checked.

security.title: Each role only sees what is its own.
security.body: Login returns a JWT inside an HttpOnly cookie, which the page's JavaScript cannot read. Role-based access rules live in the Spring Security configuration; ownership checks, in the services. In development, Vite forwards /api to Spring, so front end and API share the same origin, with no open CORS.
security.codeText: Customers and agents have their own routes, and everything else requires login. Allowing /error was a fix: without it, a denied access (403) turned into "session expired" (401), and only the end-to-end test showed it.
security.tableTitle: Security tests, with the API running
rows: Secrets in the browser build and in the git history
Calls without a cookie and with a forged-signature token
João reading, changing and canceling Marina's request
Customer on an agent route and agent on a customer route
Same message and same time (78 and 75 ms)

quality.title: Measured on the running system, not read from the code.
quality.body: Before delivery, a whole task went to verification: a code review, security tests with every role and a visual measurement that logged in as each role and went through 12 screens at 3 widths. GitHub CI runs the API tests and the front end's lint, tests and build on every pull request.

suites.title: API tests
suites.text: JUnit 5 and MockMvc: every request transition, the income limit, contract and credit, permissions per role, isolation between customers and the migrations.

suites.title: Front-end tests
suites.text: Vitest and Testing Library on screens and components, with Biome for formatting and lint.

suites.title: End-to-end flows
suites.text: Playwright in Chrome and Firefox: from sign-up to contract, rejection, modification, cancellation and each role's access.

quality.findingsTitle: What the verification found and fixed
quality.findingsBody: Of the 9 code review findings, 7 were fixed and 2 were recorded as limitations. The measurement found three more defects.

findings.title: A contract could take another company's car
findings.text: The test checked the role, not the owner. Now only the company that owns the car becomes its owner, with a test for that case.

findings.title: Concurrent conflicts returned a 500
findings.text: Two requests violating the same database constraint returned 500. They now return 409, with "This data changed while you were saving".

findings.title: Login timing revealed users
findings.text: A nonexistent user answered faster. BCrypt now runs in both cases: 78 ms versus 75 ms.

findings.title: One query per row
findings.text: The request and contract lists ran one query per row. Fixed with @EntityGraph in the repositories.

findings.title: Layout shifting on phones
findings.text: On the New request screen, the date panel was pushed down when the list arrived: a CLS of 0.292. After the fix, 0.001.

findings.title: Small touch targets
findings.text: Fields and buttons were 32 to 40 px. On touch screens they grow to 44 px; on a computer, the design did not change.

quality.tableTitle: Performance and accessibility, on the production build
rows: Slowest LCP on a phone, 4× slower CPU and simulated 4G

items.title: Check the owner, not just the role
items.text: The most serious defect slipped through the tests because they checked the user type, not who owned the car. Authorization asks two questions.

items.title: End-to-end tests catch what unit tests miss
items.text: MockMvc showed 403; the browser got 401, because Spring forwards the error to /error. Only the real flow revealed it.

items.title: The model is a living document
items.text: Three versions of the diagrams, without overwriting the earlier ones, show what changed and why. In the end, the model matches the code.

roadmap.title: What is left for when it gets published.
roadmap.body: The deliverable was the repository, with no deployment. These points were recorded in the specification and the verification:
items: A copied token stays valid until it expires (8 hours) after logout; a revoked-token list solves it.
The cookie is sent without the Secure flag so login works over local http; with HTTPS, a setting turns it on.
There is no rate limit on the login route.
Two requests for the same car in the same period are accepted for now: an open point taken to the professor.
Deploy front end and API with HTTPS, HSTS and CSP headers and a privacy policy before handling real CPF and income data.

stack.title: Java on the back, React on the front, PostgreSQL on Supabase.
stack.process: The API starts with no configuration in the local profile, on H2, for whoever grades it. With the .env filled in, it goes to Supabase: Flyway creates the tables and sample data, and a migration turns on RLS for every table so Supabase's public API does not expose the data.

closing.title: From the assignment to the contract, with every rule tested.
closing.text: It is the project where I worked the most on the back end: modeling the domain, protecting every route and proving with tests that the assignment's rules hold beyond the screen.

quaquadro.docTitle: Quaquadro, case study | Victor Cândido Leite
quaquadro.kicker: website for my own business · astro · 2026
quaquadro.title: Quaquadro
quaquadro.tagline: A website that turns a visit into an order ready on WhatsApp.
quaquadro.intro: Quaquadro turns customers' photos into printed, framed illustrations, and I do everything: customer service, drawing, printing, framing and delivery. I rebuilt the website from scratch to reach people who do not know me yet, with the origami duck identity and a guided order that ends on WhatsApp.

meta.value: Quaquadro · illustrated prints from photos · Greater Belo Horizonte · A4 for R$ 100 and 50 × 40 cm for R$ 160

problem.title: Selling prints to people who do not know me yet.
problem.body: Quaquadro started when a marketing colleague saw my work as a video editor and trusted me to make a framed print, even though I had never made one. The name joins the duck's "qua qua", my symbol since my editing days, with "quadro", Portuguese for frame. Until now, almost every customer was a coworker, with no marketing at all.

options.title: The old site
options.text: It was a first-semester college assignment. Only the images, prices, Instagram and phone number survived.

options.title: Loose orders
options.text: Every WhatsApp conversation started from scratch: size, style, deadline and city asked one by one.

options.title: The usual print shop site
options.text: A storefront of finished products with a generic shop feel, the opposite of a print made from a moment of your own.

problem.goal: within seconds, visitors understand what is sold and how much it costs, and leave with an order ready on my WhatsApp.

decisions.title: Small on purpose.
decisions.body: Every choice started from the size of the business: one person, a few orders and no monthly cost that does not pay for itself.

items.title: A guided order that ends on WhatsApp
items.text: The art only exists after the photos and the approval, so there is no ready-made product to buy. The site organizes the order and the conversation continues on WhatsApp.

items.title: No photos stored on the site
items.text: Storing photos of people, children included, would bring costs and LGPD (Brazil's data protection law) obligations. Customers send photos straight in the chat.

items.title: Payment by link, after the art
items.text: A single payment by link, with Pix or card, only after the art is approved. No deposit and no payment gateway on the site.

items.title: Astro, no React
items.text: The page is static and good for SEO. The only interaction, the order, is plain TypeScript, and the order is a single object: changing its destination does not require rebuilding the screen.

items.title: CSS animation
items.text: The headline stroke and the frame that assembles on scroll are CSS and plain TypeScript, with no animation library.

items.title: Cloudflare instead of Vercel
items.text: Vercel's free plan forbids commercial use, and the paid one costs US$ 20 a month. On Cloudflare, every push to main goes live in about 3 minutes.

identity.title: The colors came from the duck's folds.
identity.body: The symbol is an origami duck, drawn as a vector. The palette was measured on its folds: a light site in pastel tones, with no dark sections, and darks that go almost to black to give the text contrast. Each color has a set use, and the ones below 4.5:1 never become small text.
identity.note: The gallery prints are composited from each artwork's vector onto empty wall-and-floor scenes. The logo typeface is commercial, so the logo is a vector and the text uses Outfit.

order.body: The order is the only part with logic. It lives in a single file, with tests: price by size, a 2-week minimum deadline in the Brasília time zone and the message built from the customer's choices.

steps.text: Size, style, people, occasion, deadline and city, with a live preview and price.

steps.title: Check
steps.text: Name, city and deadline validated on screen; a date outside the range is cleared when leaving the field.

steps.title: Reminder
steps.text: A Cloudflare function creates the reminder in my Notion calendar without holding the customer back.

steps.title: WhatsApp
steps.text: The chat opens with the message ready. Photos go there.

order.codeMessageTitle: The message comes from the order
order.codeMessageText: Only what the customer filled in goes in, and the price comes from the chosen size. Without JavaScript, the button still opens WhatsApp.
order.codeApiTitle: The function that creates the reminder
order.codeApiText: It refuses requests from another origin, limits sending to 5 per minute and ignores bots with an invisible field only they fill in.

quality.title: Measured on the production build.
quality.body: Before launch, a whole verification phase: speed, contrast in pixels, scrolling at several widths, links, secrets and dependencies.
rows: npm audit and secrets in the repository
quality.findingsTitle: What the verification found and fixed

findings.title: Opening button not clickable
findings.text: An invisible paper layer sat on top of it. It was missing pointer-events: none.

findings.title: Zero width on a phone in landscape
findings.text: The opening's calculation produced a negative height. In that orientation it now uses the column layout.

findings.title: Wrong preview after reload
findings.text: The browser restored the size choice, but the preview did not follow.

findings.title: Page dragging sideways
findings.text: The iPhone date field has its own width and the closed menu sat off screen. minmax(0, 1fr) columns and the closed menu with display: none.

findings.title: No link preview on WhatsApp
findings.text: The configured address pointed to a domain that does not exist yet. The preview image now comes from the live address.

findings.title: Small touch targets
findings.text: The logo and the Instagram link were below 44 px.

items.title: What you cannot see can still block
items.text: An invisible layer over the main button stopped the click. Only checking in the browser showed it.

items.title: The iPhone has its own rules
items.text: Its date picker ignores min and max and has its own width. Chrome never reproduced the sideways drag: the real device is the final test.

items.title: Start from the size of the business
items.text: No database, no stored photos and no gateway: less cost and less risk, and the order can change destination without rebuilding the screen.

roadmap.title: What is left before announcing it.
roadmap.body: The site is live but has not been promoted yet. These steps come first:
items: Buy the custom domain and replace the temporary Cloudflare address in the config, robots.txt and sitemap.
Validate the terms, privacy and cancellation policies with a lawyer and add the supplier details required by Brazilian e-commerce law (Decree 7,962/2013).
Align the deadline across every section and test the order and the link preview on a real iPhone.
Turn on the orders dashboard linked to the spreadsheet, already deployed and switched off until the credentials are ready.

stack.title: Static in front, one function behind.
stack.process: Astro generates the page and Cloudflare serves it. The only server-side part is the order function, with Cloudflare's native rate limiting. Print images are generated from the original vectors by a script, already optimized.

closing.title: From the duck to the order.
closing.text: It is the project where I was both the client and the developer: deciding what the business needs, cutting what does not pay for itself and shipping a fast site that is already live.
